components.text: Whether the privation-of-good argument establishes that goodness requires a divine standard.
The decisive demand is whether goodness requires a divine ground.
Whether identifying as a nonbeliever removes every burden from the atheist's broader explanatory claims.
The qualification that independently asserted positive claims incur their own burden of proof.
The decisive demand is whether the defended atheist position makes positive claims requiring support.
Whether agnostic nonbelief itself incurs a general positive burden of proof.
The relevant demand is what positive conclusion the pro moral argument undertakes to establish.
Whether objective morality has been established rather than assumed before invoking a divine explanation.
Whether the limited conclusion still requires objective morality to be independently demonstrated.
The decisive demand is the limited conclusion that a divine ground follows from objective morality.
Whether goodness has been established as identical with God's nature.
Whether invoking a transcendent divine mind independently grounds objective wrongness without circularity.
Whether a generic divine ground can be inferred from objective morality rather than presupposed in defining it.
The decisive inference identifies goodness with God's nature and uses that goodness to infer God.
Whether even the limited divine-ground conclusion follows without assuming a transcendent mind.
Whether compelling moral judgments require mind-independent goodness and a divine standard.
Whether conditional practical rules can explain moral experience without reaching any divine ground.
The decisive demand is whether moral experience requires a divine rather than natural explanation.
Whether an evolutionary explanation of moral judgment can be accepted without undermining trust in beliefs generally.
Whether vivid moral knowledge can be displaced merely by locating judgment in evolved psychology.
The decisive demand is whether evolutionary causation explains moral belief without defeating confidence in belief generally.
Whether reason must receive a non-evolutionary validation before it can serve as a trustworthy basis for inquiry.
The decisive demand is how reason can be trusted if its validation cannot escape the same cognitive process.
Whether calling reason a necessary assumption explains its trustworthiness or the status of objective logical laws.
Whether assumption-dependent conclusions account for objective norms rather than merely applying stipulated premises.
The decisive demand is whether merely assuming reason explains its trustworthiness and objective logical norms.
Whether naturalistic evolution can account for truth-directed rational cognition.
Whether objective logical rules are compatible with reasoning whose conclusions depend on adopted assumptions.
The decisive demand is whether objective logical rules can coexist with assumption-dependent reasoning.
Whether declaring reason subjective is compatible with asserting objectively true conclusions through reasoning.
Whether reason can remain merely assumed while supporting truth claims about its own status.
The decisive claim is that reason itself is subjective despite objective logical rules.
Whether the compelling force of a judgment entails that it has the same objective status as a logical or numerical truth.
Whether instinctively powerful moral judgments establish a mind-independent standard of goodness.
The decisive demand is whether premise-dependent reasoning is self-defeating.
Whether compelling moral intuitions survive an evolutionary explanation as evidence of objective truth.
Whether immediate moral awareness can warrant objective obligation despite skeptical or culturally contingent explanations.
Whether evolutionary explanation defeats the prima facie evidential force of moral obligation.
The decisive demand is whether compelling moral awareness has evidential force despite skeptical explanations.
Whether the relevant naturalistic demand is to justify moral truth or to explain why moral experiences arise.
Whether giving a causal account of moral experience commits the speaker to deriving moral truth from evolution.
The decisive inference moves from experiencing obligation to the objective truth of that obligation.
Whether an evolutionary explanation must purport to justify or discredit every resulting belief.
Whether practical judgments that one society is better require an objective standard beyond shared attitudes.
Whether comparative moral language can remain wholly attitude-dependent across cultures.
The decisive demand is to preserve the distinction between causal explanation and moral justification.
Whether shared pursuit of a better society requires an objective external standard.
Whether emotional recoil from naturalistic moral arbitrariness establishes an objective standard or falsifies naturalism.
Whether the strength of moral feeling is sufficient to establish the objective truth of its content.
The decisive demand is whether discomfort with arbitrary morality establishes an objective external best.
Whether the compelling force of moral conviction establishes its objective truth.
Whether an evolutionary origin account can warrant belief in its own truth rather than merely describe causal production.
Whether causal explanation of thought supplies epistemic justification for accepting the explanatory theory.
Whether moral conviction is merely an assumption or may instead be treated as properly basic.
The decisive demand is whether moral conviction has epistemic status beyond emotional recoil.
Whether an evolutionary causal account can warrant confidence in its own truth.
Whether moral disagreement or lack of clarity entails that there is no objective moral reality.
Whether variation in moral judgment by itself establishes only conditional or subjective morality.
Whether epistemic difficulty should be distinguished from the ontological existence of moral facts.
The decisive issue is whether variation or discomfort establishes that objective morality is unreal.
Whether cultural disagreement and unclear cases negate an objective moral reality.
